label: instances and discussions about majority and minority perspectives
explanation: Lexical feature for the word "majority". Peak lands on the " majority"/" Majority" token in any sense (statistical, political title, court opinion, sentence-initial): 0.80-0.86 of max in my prompts, up to 1.0 in top examples. Weaker tiers: "majorities" (on "ities") 0.55; " minority" 0.37; "preponderance" 0.33; "plurality" 0.24-0.29; "Minorities", "bulk", pre-modifier "overwhelming" 0.22-0.27; "thirds" 0.18; spillover on the following token ("of", "Leader") 0.15-0.25. Does NOT fire: "Most" (0.05), "major", "minor", "half", "multiple", "mostly", and presumably code/math/unrelated prose. Causal: ablating it after "the majority held ... while the" halved " minority" (0.59 to 0.29), KL 0.22.
causal: Zero-ablating 16333 on "The court was divided: the majority held that the statute applied, while the" (active at " majority", act 48.3) dropped next-token " minority" from 0.592 to 0.288 and raised " dissent" from 0.208 to 0.367, KL 0.224.
examples_explanation: Token-level feature for the word "majority": every top example peaks on " majority" (the/a/vast/mass majority, legal "majority" vs dissent), all at near-max activation, and the direction promotes majority/Majority. Expect strong firing on any " majority" token regardless of context. Likely weaker firing on close relatives: "minority" (in promotes list, lower rank) and possibly "plurality" as a quantifier. Should NOT fire on code, math, LaTeX, biology text, or generic quantity words without the majority token ("some of which", numbers).
surprises: The only firing miss in all three sets was the random sentence "Antioxidant activities of the water-soluble fraction in tempeh-", predicted 0 but barely firing at rel 0.105 with peak_token " fraction". Largest magnitude gaps: "the vast majority of parents whose children" was predicted 8-9 but came in at rel 0.644 (peak_token " majority"), and "ethnic minority groups. We" was predicted 6 by the label set but was rel 0.257 (peak_token " minority").

label: elements related to programming structures and their definitions
explanation: Fires on the indentation-whitespace token that opens a class body: the indent right after a Python `class X(Base):` header line. Tiers: 0.85-0.9 of max inside a clean Python file (also 0.83 on the later indent before the first method); 0.6 on the deeper indent after a nested class; 0.3 with a truncated header or mixed-language context; 0.1-0.27 for Elixir module-body indent/`@` and for one-line class headers with no newline (`):`, `=`, `:`). Does not fire: function-body indents, C++ templates, Rust attributes, structs, C# methods (all <0.1), prose. Ablation: KL 0.035, small effect. Caveats: a fifth run_prompt was blocked by the permission classifier and never ran; probe 3 was structurally close to pool items 5 and 15.
causal: Zero-ablating the feature on my own prompt "import sys / class Parser(Base): / indent" (active at 45.96 on the indent token) barely changed the next-token distribution (KL 0.035): `def` fell 0.62 -> 0.55, the docstring quote rose 0.17 -> 0.19 and `pass` entered the top 6, so the model relies on it only weakly here.
examples_explanation: Every top example peaks on the indentation whitespace token immediately after a Python class header line ("class Name(Base):\n" then the 4-space indent), i.e. the position where the class body or docstring is about to start. The promoted tokens (triple quotes, "#![", BOM+"#") are body-opening or file-opening tokens, which fits. I expect strong firing on the indent after "class X(Y):" in Python, weaker firing on analogous body-start positions in other languages (Elixir "module ... do", C++ "{"), and nothing on prose, math, hex constants, PHP statement bodies or Rust doc attributes. The label's "programming structures" is much broader than what the examples show. Not tested: only one feature_info call was made.
surprises: Investigated's own probe "import os class Scheduler(Thread): \"\"\"Runs queued jobs on a timer.\"\"\"" was predicted 8.5 but reached only rel 0.083 (peak_token "):", not fired; the tool's echoed text shows the newlines/indent collapsed to spaces), and "template<typename T> void test_minres_T() {" was predicted 1 by investigated and examples but fired at rel 0.187 on "<"; all held-out class rows fired weakly (rel 0.13-0.25, peaks on " =", " @", " def", " class") against expectations of 5-8. Every whitespace-only "on" value came back as null in the rows, so investigated's peak_hit of 1 rests only on the two "@" rows (" @" in "module PubSub do @behaviour Absinthe.Subscription.Pubsub" and the defmodule probe) and examples' peak_hit of 0 only on its "do" guess.

label: dialogue or conversational exchanges
explanation: Fires on the first 1-4 words of a reply turn in back-and-forth dialogue: the opening of a quoted or speaker-labelled utterance that responds to the previous speaker. Strongest (0.7-1.0 of max) on rebuttal/echo openers ("But you promised", "You did not", "They are", "What moments"); mid (0.35-0.55) on other reply openers ("That's fine", "Because", "you believe" in a Q line); weak (0.15-0.3) on first-turn openers, one-word answers ("No", "Yes"), Japanese script replies. Zero on narration, reported speech, embedded non-dialogue quotes, addresses, code. Decays within a few tokens of the turn start. Causally weak: ablation barely moves next-token probabilities (KL 0.006), though the greedy continuation changed.
causal: Zero-ablating 9261 on “You said you would be home by nine.” “But you gave KL 0.0058 at the final position: top next tokens only reshuffled (" said" 0.146 -> 0.134, " know" 0.129 -> 0.153), which flipped the greedy completion from "said you would be home by eight" to "know I'm always late", so the feature's effect on output is small.
examples_explanation: Only two distinct top examples, both showing the same thing: the opening words of a reply turn in quoted dialogue, right after another speaker's quotation closes (”  “What [[moments]]?”, ”\n\n“[[But]] you made). Peak is on the first content tokens of the response, especially a rejoinder that picks up or challenges the previous speaker. Similar features (witness testimony responses, dialogue and quotations) suggest transcript Q/A turns fire too, more weakly. Expect no firing on code, addresses, patent boilerplate, news prose or narrative without a speaker change; a lone quotation without a preceding turn should be weak or silent. The promotes list is code-identifier noise and uninformative.
surprises: All three sets missed the weak firing on "gets you on an \"of interest\" list._ ...or your association with" (rel 0.131, peak_token "or"; expected 0.5-1), and "\"Q So then you would further state..." fired weaker than predicted (rel 0.258, peak_token " then" vs expected 3-5 on "Q"/"So"/"you"). Peak tokens were often off by one within the opener: "Me: “They’re afraid—" peaked on "re" (rel 0.878, not "Me"/"They"), "That's very good" peaked on "That" (rel 0.842, investigated said "s" with expected 5.5), and the agent sentence "THE COURT: You may step down now." peaked on " You" not "may".

label: patterns and structures in the text
explanation: Fires inside long horizontal-rule / separator runs of one repeated punctuation character (---- ==== //// **** ____ ~~~~ #### ....), as in code comment banners and document dividers. The first 16-char chunk of a run is ~0 (0-0.07); the second chunk is 0.5-0.75 of max and the third 0.6-0.95 (peak), then it decays (0.1-0.3) toward the line end. Weaker tiers: ;;;; runs 0.3-0.4, repeated letters "aaaa" ~0.24, "-=-=" ~0.4, spaced "* * *" ~0.1. Does NOT fire on short runs (----, ========), table rules |-----|, repeated digits, ordinary prose or code, or the words "pattern"/"structure". Ablating it mid-rule barely matters: P(another 16-dash chunk) 0.68 -> 0.78, KL 0.055, so it mildly pushes toward ending the rule.
causal: Zero-ablating the feature on a prompt ending three 16-dash chunks into a "//------" comment rule (acts 3.9, 44.8, 57.4) raised P(next = another 16-dash chunk) from 0.68 to 0.78 with KL 0.055, a small effect consistent with the feature mildly promoting the end of the rule (newline) rather than driving its continuation.
examples_explanation: Fires on long horizontal separator/rule lines made of one repeated character (----, ====, ////, ****), mostly code-comment banners. The top examples all peak on a 16-character chunk partway into the run (after roughly 32 characters), so the run must be long; activation builds with length. I expect it to generalise, somewhat weaker, to other repeated-character rules (;;;;, ____) and to rules outside code (LaTeX/markdown/legal dividers). It should NOT fire on ordinary prose, code identifiers, SQL, HTML, names, citations, or short punctuation. Label "patterns and structures in the text" is too vague; the real trigger is the divider line itself.
surprises: No firing/non-firing disagreements in any set; the largest magnitude miss is ") ;;; End initial eval-region ;;;;..." (peak_token ";;;;", rel 0.32), predicted 6 by label and 5 by examples versus 3 by investigated. Next is "______... On appeal from the 44th District Court" (peak_token "________________", rel 0.57) and "_DATA_HPP */ ////..." (peak_token "////////////////", rel 0.758) which examples over-predicted at 9.

label: transitional phrases that indicate the passage of time
explanation: Token detector for the word "later", not a general time-transition feature. Sentence-initial "Later" is strongest (0.75-1.0 of max); mid-sentence adverbial "later" ("later that night", "much later", "a later version", "see you later") 0.6-0.8; "N weeks later" and "sooner or later" weaker (0.2-0.45). The token right after "later" carries spillover (0.2-0.35). Weak tier, 0.12-0.3: afterward(s), Subsequently, Earlier, late, latter, latest. Does NOT fire: then, eventually, soon, after, next day, ago, previously, recently, today, early, last season, code. Causal: zero-ablating on a prompt ending "Two hours" changed nothing (KL 0, no active positions): it reads the token "later" rather than predicting it, despite its decoder promoting "later".
causal: Zero-ablating feature 9739 on "We met for coffee at noon and talked for an hour. Two hours" left the next-token distribution unchanged (" later" 0.715 before and after, KL 0) because the feature was not active at any position, so it detects the token "later" on input rather than driving its prediction.
examples_explanation: Fires on the token "later" itself. All top examples are sentence-initial "Later" ("Later on I", "Later, in August", "Later that day") right after a full stop or paragraph break, and the direction promotes later/Later/afterward. I expect capitalised sentence-initial "Later" at full strength, lowercase mid-sentence "later" ("later verified", "later on") somewhat weaker, and possibly a weak response on the related "late". Should NOT fire on code, email/contact text, or prose without "later", including other time words ("Every year", "today") and the look-alike "latter". Density (0.00076) is close to the frequency of "later" alone, so little beyond that token.
surprises: The label and examples sets both missed "'s definition of the latter is" (expected 0 and 1, actual rel 0.23, peak_token " latter"), the only recall miss; investigated predicted it correctly at 2. The label set also underrated "— a fact later verified in The Post's" (expected 5, actual rel 0.885, peak_token " later"), where mid-sentence "later" fired about as strongly as sentence-initial "Later".

label: keywords related to corporate social responsibility and ethical business practices
explanation: Fires on the theme of ethical/sustainable production and consumption (fair trade, ethical sourcing, recycled, pesticide-free, living wages, labor rights, wildlife protection), not on a single word. Once the theme starts it stays on across the following tokens, including function words and punctuation. Tiers: ~1.0 of max on "ethical sourcing" / "fair" (trade) in a list of green virtues; 0.5-0.75 on recycled, pesticide, rights, protection, sustainability; ~0.15-0.2 on handmade-vs-factory talk. Does NOT fire on "fair"/"responsible" in a courtroom sense, climate-science description (melting glaciers), code, math, citations or medicine. Causal: ablation barely changed the next-token prediction (KL 0.009), slightly lowering " sourced".
causal: Zero-ablating feature 11469 on "Our coffee beans are vegan-friendly, pesticide-free and ethically" (active at 25.6 on " ethically") left the next-token distribution almost unchanged (KL 0.0087): " sourced" fell from 0.709 to 0.684 while " grown" rose from 0.031 to 0.048, so the model barely relies on it here.
examples_explanation: Fires on ethical/sustainable-production vocabulary in consumer or business contexts: descriptors like "fairtrade", "responsible manufacturing", organic, ecology, human rights, ethical/social/environmental responsibility. Strongest on the ethical adjective inside a list of such virtues ("vegan, organic and [[fair]]trade"). Promoted outputs (sustainable, sourcing, suppliers, carbon) support a sustainability/ethical-sourcing reading rather than corporate jargon alone. Expected NOT to fire on code, LaTeX, legal citations, chat logs, clinical or medical text, author names, or pure chemistry/toxicology without an ethical-consumption frame (PBDEs is at most marginal). Peak-token guesses in the pool are uncertain: the examples only show the peak landing on the ethical descriptor itself.
surprises: "made with love, instead of in factories, without a thought." fired at rel 0.558 with peak_token "," while all sets predicted only 1-3 (label missed it as non-firing), and "ecology and human rights but maybe that will go with a renewal of custom-made and" was predicted 5 on "rights" in every set but reached only rel 0.179 with peak_token " and". "inated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs) have been described" fired at rel 0.18 (peak_token "s") against predictions of 0-1 in all three sets, the one shared recall miss.

label: references to health-related topics, particularly viruses and diseases
explanation: The label is wrong. The feature is a mid-text <bos> detector: a literal <bos> token appearing after other text (a document boundary) fires at 0.65-0.80 of max (52.5, 42.8, 53.1 of 65.5), matching all 8 top examples. Otherwise it is near-silent, with weak sporadic firing on a few rare proper-noun tokens: " Zika" 0.11-0.23, "bola" (Ebola) 0.20, "riche" (Barrichello) 0.12, " Python" 0.08, " Java" 0.06, "engue" 0.05. Does NOT fire: virus, disease, HIV, hepatitis, influenza, malaria, SARS, gene names, acronyms, code, "Q:" without <bos>, ordinary prose. Causally inert: ablating it at <bos> left next-token predictions unchanged (KL 0.0002).
causal: Zero-ablating the feature on a prompt with a mid-text <bos> (act 53.1 there, 5.4 on " Python") left the next-token distribution essentially unchanged (top token "\n\n" 0.8605 -> 0.859, KL 0.0002), so the model does not rely on it for the following prediction.
examples_explanation: All eight top examples peak on a literal <bos> token appearing mid-text (document boundary), regardless of topic: code, Q&A, math, medical. Density (~1/138 tokens) matches one BOS per context window, so this is mainly a BOS/document-start feature; the health label looks like an artifact of surrounding text. No pool sentence contains a mid-text <bos>, so most should be silent. Hedge: the pool has two biomedical sentences (virus, BRAF mutation), which suggests a weak secondary response to virus/disease/genetics vocabulary, so I predict those fire weakly. Not expected to fire: code, math, finance, food, sport, art, general prose.
surprises: All three sets predicted 0 on held-out rows that fired on proper-noun/acronym tokens: "entitled Sally Mann: A Thousand Crossings" (rel 0.376, peak_token " Mann"), "CIBC CreditSmart" (0.207, "IBC"), "the UAE points to the WMO" (0.122, " UAE"); the label set also expected 8 on "![Virus proliferation analyses" but it only reached 0.165 with peak on "ENV" (DENV2), not "Virus". In the investigated set the agent sentence "Measles, malaria and influenza are infectious diseases" was predicted 0 but fired at 0.292 on peak_token "les" (Measles), while the <bos> sentence matched (expected 8, rel 0.797, peak "<bos>").

label: mentions of specific individuals and their actions or roles within a narrative
explanation: Fires on a referent standing as the grammatical subject of a clause, just before its verb, usually after a comma/conjunction/"that"/"when". Strongest on person or company names and capitalised epithets ("the Butcher"): 0.4-0.53 of max in my tests (top examples reach 1.0); multi-token names peak on the last fragment. Names as objects ~0.24; role nouns as subjects (teacher, trainee, supervisor) 0.17-0.31; a chemical name 0.2; the following verb often 0.1-0.3. Does NOT fire on pronouns, place names (even as subject), a name as the very first token, code or maths. Causal: ablation at a subject name barely changed next-token predictions (KL 0.005), so the feature is a weak readout there.
causal: Zero-ablating the feature on "...and in the end Harlan" (active only on " Harlan", act 13.4) left the next-token distribution essentially unchanged (" decided" 0.088 to 0.086, " County" 0.052 to 0.063), KL 0.0053.
examples_explanation: Fires on the name (or title-like designation) of a specific agent standing as the grammatical subject of a clause, just before its verb: "the [[Conqueror]] removed", "and [[Napier]]", "that [[Grant]] did not", "Gen[[mar]] Kansas was not", "and [[Joshua]] couldn't". Peak is on the name token (final fragment of a multi-token name). Promoted tokens are subject-following verbs (decided, chose, wanted). Common in narrative and legal prose. Expect no firing on code, math, numbers, generic scientific/abstract prose, and little on pronouns, common-noun subjects, or place names in non-subject position.
surprises: The investigated explanation's "does NOT fire on pronouns or place names" claim was wrong: agent sentences "and then she decided to sell it" (expected 0, rel 0.271, peak_token " she") and "Portugal agreed to return the islands" (expected 0.5, rel 0.25, peak_token " Portugal") both fired, as did heldout "that she lacks the normal amount" (expected 0.5, rel 0.168, peak " she") and "in Šeduva were closed" (rel 0.139, peak "va"). It also predicted 2 on "When CdTB precursor" (actual 0, a false positive), and "There Hassan would be waiting" peaked on " would" rather than "Hassan" in all sets.

label: terms related to payment processing and financial transactions
explanation: Lexical feature for the noun "payment". Tiers (fraction of max 32.4): " payment"/" Payment"/line-initial "Payment" 0.85-1.0; plural " payments" ~0.6; "payment" as a subword or in "repayment", "prepayment", "nonpayment" 0.45-0.57; weak synonyms 0.12-0.26 ("installment", "payout", "remittance", "invoice", "disbursement"); "due" right after payment ~0.1. Does NOT fire on the verb forms "pay", "paid", "paying", nor on "owe", "fee", "deposit", "cash", "credit card", "transaction", "refund", "PayPal", "salary" or dollar amounts, so the label's "financial transactions" is too broad. Causal: zero-ablating it on a prompt ending in " payment" (act 29.7) barely changed the next-token distribution (KL 0.0018; methods 0.544 to 0.538), so its output effect there is negligible.
causal: Zero-ablating feature 13087 on "We accept credit cards, checks and several other payment" (active only on " payment", act 29.7) left the next-token prediction essentially unchanged (methods 0.544 to 0.538, options 0.304 to 0.313), KL 0.0018.
examples_explanation: Token-level feature for the word "payment" itself (Payment/payment/payments, any casing), not finance in general. All top examples peak on the "payment" token, either as a section heading ("Payment Options", "Payment Notices") or in "payment processing"; the promotes list is nothing but payment/Payments variants. Expect strong firing on any literal "payment(s)" token, possibly weaker on close morphological relatives ("repayment", "paying", "paid"). Expect NO firing on general money or transaction text without that word (dollar amounts, contracts, "owe", fees), nor on unrelated code, science, sports or pet text.
surprises: All three sets predicted 0 on two held-out sentences that fired weakly with no payment word: "To check whether the packets are being correctly formed and received" (peak_token " packets", rel 0.273) and "so that it has a specific probability? Or at least on certain days" (peak_token " probability", rel 0.297). The label set also under-called "on the payment free period and the repayment period" (expected 5, actual rel 0.863 on " payment"); the set-level peak_hit is reported as 1 even though those two missed rows carry peak_hit=false.

label: copyright symbols and copyright-related text
explanation: Fires on the copyright SYMBOL that follows the word "Copyright" in source-file header comments, not on the word itself. Tiers (fraction of max): "Copyright ©" in a // header ~0.94 on " ©"; "Copyright (c)" ~0.46-0.56 on "c" (")" ~0.4-0.48, "(" ~0.2-0.3); uppercase "(C)" ~0.34-0.37; lowercase "copyright (c)" ~0.22; "COPYRIGHT (c)", bare "©", bare "(c) 2015", "©" ~0.15-0.23; weak spill on following year digits (<=0.18). Does NOT fire: the word "Copyright" alone, "Copyright 2020" without symbol (~0.05), "@copyright", prose about copyright law, "(c)" as list option or f(c) (0-0.07), ordinary prose/code. Causal: ablating at "Copyright ©" collapses the next-token prediction of the space before the year (0.999 -> 0.17), KL 1.79.
causal: Zero-ablating 4409 on "//  Created by Sam on 3/4/19.\n//  Copyright ©" (act 71.5 on " ©") dropped the next-token probability of the space preceding the year from 0.999 to 0.17 and made " Sam" the top prediction (0.69), KL 1.787, so the feature carries the "symbol seen, year comes next" signal.
examples_explanation: Fires on the copyright mark that directly follows the word "Copyright" in source-file header comments: strongest on the "©" symbol (top examples, ~76), weaker on the "c" inside "(c)" (~44, about 0.57 of max). The pool has no "©", only "(c)"/"(C)", so I expect mid-strength peaks on the letter inside the parentheses, slightly lower for uppercase "(C)". The word "Copyright" itself, the year and the holder name are not the peak. Not expected to fire: ordinary prose, code without a copyright line, maths, install logs, or related IP words such as "patents" with no copyright notice.
surprises: All three sets missed the held-out row "try: while 1: time.sleep(1" (expected 0, actual rel 0.208, peak_token "1"), a non-copyright firing that no explanation covers; the label set also over-predicted the "Copyright (c)" rows (expected 8 vs rel 0.44-0.50, peak_token "c"), and "// Copyright © 2021 Blue Harbor Software" came in at rel 0.781 on " ©" vs 9 expected. The label set's peak_hit of 0.8 looks inflated: its on="Copyright" was scored as a hit against peak_token "c" on four rows (apparently a substring match), though the label never named the symbol.

label: terms related to medical conditions, particularly types of dementia and immune cell characteristics
explanation: Noisy, context-dependent feature for biomedical research prose, firing sporadically on disease/immune-cell nouns. Strongest on "dementia" in clinical/epidemiology text (top examples 1.0; my tests 0.5-0.63 after "Late-onset"/"Young-onset", on "dementias", and "predicts dementia") and on leukocyte terms after a tissue modifier (top examples 0.85; my "lymphocytes" 0.42). Weak tier 0.15-0.35: digits in CD markers, "decline", "mice", "expansions", "onset", following "was"/"(". Does NOT fire: lay-register "has dementia", "vascular dementia" (0), "Mucosal leukocytes" (0), monocytes, macrophages, tumor/cortex, dental terms, non-medical hyphenated compounds, code, math. Firing is unreliable even on the same word. Causal: ablation is essentially null (KL 0.002).
causal: Zero-ablating feature 276 on "...dementias in a rural county. Young-onset dementia" (active at 11.5 on the final token) left next-token predictions essentially unchanged (" (" 0.342 -> 0.348, " was" 0.318 -> 0.325), KL 0.002, so the model does not measurably rely on it there.
examples_explanation: Top examples show only two contexts: "dementia" after "Early-onset", and "leuk/ocytes" after "Lamina propria" (subject of "were isolated/harvested"). So the trigger looks like the head noun of a modified biomedical noun phrase naming a disease or cell population, strongest on cell-type words ending in -ocytes and on "dementia". The promotes list is uninformative noise and similar features have low cosine, so the generalisation beyond these two phrases is a guess: I expect weaker firing on other cell types (lymphocytes, hepatocytes, cells) and disease nouns (tumor, caries). I expect no firing on code, math/LaTeX, addresses, dialogue, or general non-medical prose.
surprises: The investigated set predicted 1 (no fire) for "medullary tumor which had no relation with the cerebellar cortex" but it fired at rel 0.561 on peak_token " tumor" (the explanation explicitly said tumor/cortex does not fire), and also missed "microleakage, marginal discoloration ... secondary caries" (rel 0.183, peak_token "leak"). All three sets missed "be the Lévy measure having $f$" (rel 0.169, peak_token " Lé"), and on "CD11c+ cells with infected hepatocytes" the peak was " cells" (rel 0.547), not "CD" or "1" as label/investigated predicted.

label: punctuation marks and other non-word tokens
explanation: Not general punctuation. Main trigger: a <bos> token appearing mid-text (document boundary), 0.65-0.77 of max in my tests, 1.0 in top examples. Secondary: the "." after Go test-assertion package names: "require." 0.45-0.5 inside a real test function, 0.16-0.2 in a jumble, "expect." 0.14. Flaky: ":" in "<xsl:" (0-0.2, stronger on a repeat). Does NOT fire: prose, sentence punctuation, "error:", comment stars and "*/", LaTeX, "fmt.", "os.", "self.", "check.", "std::". Causal: zero-ablation is near-null (KL 0.0023). Caveat: only 3 run_prompts ran; a fourth, plain-prose test was blocked by the permission classifier as too close to pool sentences, so prose zeros rest on one sentence plus density 0.00045.
causal: Zero-ablating the feature on a Go test snippet ending in a mid-text <bos> (act 25.4 there, 20.0 and 17.5 on the two "require." dots) left the next-token distribution essentially unchanged (KL 0.0023; "\n" 0.204 -> 0.220, "1" 0.178 -> 0.168; log-prob deltas at the dots +0.009 and -0.08), so the model barely relies on it here.
examples_explanation: The label is misleading. All eight top examples peak on a mid-context <bos> token (a document boundary inside the window), after ends such as "/* END */", "#endif" or a Category line. None of the pool sentences shows a mid-text <bos>, so no strong activation is expected. My guess for weak firing is code residue: comment terminators "*/" and end-of-statement code such as "assert.Nil(t, err)"; this rests on the promoted tokens (closing bracket plus period) and code-like similar features, not on any example. Ordinary prose, names, dates and recipe text should not fire. Confidence is low for every non-zero prediction.
surprises: Label set's worst misses were random-pool punctuation rows predicted to fire that were dead zero, e.g. "updating set that sends messages immediately * ****...*/" (expected 6, rel 0, peak_token "updating") and "r+2)} - \frac{1}{r+2} =" (expected 5, rel 0, peak_token "r"). Investigated set's only miss was the agent sentence "fmt.Println(total) os.path.join(base, name) self.assertEqual(left, right) check.Equal(a, b)" (expected 0, actual rel 0.122, peak_token "."), so the claimed non-firing on fmt./os./self./check. is slightly wrong.

label: concise summaries and key points within a larger text
explanation: Fires on the final word of sentence-initial summarising/reformulating discourse markers, strongest on "short" in "In short" (0.6-0.7 of max; 0.33 when followed by a colon late in a marker-heavy text) and "put" in "Simply put" (0.68), with spillover on the following comma. Tiers: "In brief" 0.55; "In other words" 0.4; "nutshell" 0.34; "To sum up" 0.26; "In general" 0.23; mid-sentence "basically" 0.16-0.22; "Essentially"/"Generally" 0.14-0.2; headers like "Key Points:"/"Takeaways:"/"Summary" 0.14-0.18. It is lexical, not semantic: "In short order" still fires 0.62. Does NOT fire on adjective "short" ("a short walk"), "said in a ...", recipes, code. Causal: ablation at "In short" barely moves next-token prediction (KL 0.005).
causal: Zero-ablating feature 970 on "... the camera is blurry. In short" (active only on " short", act 30.1) barely changed the next-token distribution: "," 0.946 -> 0.960 and ":" 0.036 -> 0.022, KL 0.0047, so the model does not rely on it for the immediate next token.
examples_explanation: Fires on sentence-initial summarising/reformulating discourse markers, peaking on the final word of the marker just before the comma: "In [[short]]", "Simply [[put]]", "Simply [[stated]]". Promotes "Basically", "Essentially", "nutshell", "in other words" equivalents, so it marks "a condensed restatement is coming". Expect strong firing on "In short" (even "In short order", since the peak token precedes "order"), moderate on "In other words" and mid-sentence "basically", weak on "In general". Should NOT fire on code, citations, chemical notation, patent prose, quoted statements, tweets, or actual summary content lacking such a marker; "Talking Points:" is likely near zero.
surprises: The only false positive was "...let sit. Talking Points:" (actual 0, peak_token "."), predicted 5 by label and 2 by investigated, so the header tier of the explanation did not hold here. "In short order, Calvin" fired strongest of all (rel 0.872, peak_token " short") but was under-predicted at 5-6 by label/investigated, and "In other words, Rule 59(e) is" fired 0.569 on " words" against expected 4.

label: comparative and superlative adjectives to identify effectiveness and performance metrics
explanation: Fires on superlative/extremum-ranking words that single out one member of a compared set, peaking on the superlative token. Strongest on "highest" in "X showed/had the highest [metric]" (0.6-0.8 of max; top examples 1.0), also "lowest" (0.55), "greatest" (0.46), "ranked first" and "the most [noun]" (0.65-0.7). Weaker: "largest" (0.26), "most frequently" (0.28), "worst/smallest" (0.25), "most common" (0.2). Preceding "the" and the following noun carry 0.15-0.35 spillover. Does NOT fire (<=0.1): comparatives ("higher than", "greater" ~0.1), "best", "top", "maximum", "peaked", plain "high", "of major importance", code. Label's "comparative" and "effectiveness" parts are wrong. Causal: ablation barely changes next-token predictions (KL 0.014).
causal: Zero-ablating 2011 on "Among all the schools surveyed, students in Kenya reported the highest" (act 30.1 on " highest", 0.81 of max) left the next-token distribution nearly unchanged (KL 0.0144; " levels" 0.198 -> 0.190, " rates" 0.076 -> 0.102), so the feature detects superlatives but has little direct effect on the immediate prediction.
examples_explanation: Fires on the superlative token itself in quantity-ranking statements: " highest" (also " greatest") in "showed/had the highest level/proportion/efficacy of ...", mostly scientific or statistical prose. All top examples peak on the superlative, before the measured noun. Expect weaker firing on other superlatives/comparatives of degree ("most often", "higher"), and little on plain "great". Should NOT fire on code, general narrative, non-comparative adjectives, or text with no ranking/extreme-value word. The label's "effectiveness and performance metrics" is too narrow: the trigger is the superlative word, not the metric.
surprises: "had the highest proportion of cases." was predicted 8-10 on "highest" but reached only rel 0.24 with peak_token "." (similarly "was performed most often (34" peaked on " (" at 0.246, and agent sentence "Highest among the peaks," peaked on "," at 0.147). The investigated set's only miss was the comparative "mice scored significantly higher than WT" (expected 1, actual rel 0.159, peak_token " higher"), which the label and examples sets counted as firing.

label: occurrences of empty string or null values in code
explanation: Fires on empty-string literal tokens: a pair of quotes with nothing between, peak on the quote token itself. Tiers: code ` ""` after = or return ~0.8-1.0; variants `''`, `=""`, `"",`, `"";`, `""));`, `("")` ~0.5-0.8; HTML `=""` and prose `""`/`''` ~0.3-0.45; triple-quote closer and empty `{}` ~0.15-0.4; `" "`, `[]`, closing quotes <=0.12. Does NOT fire on null/None, 0/False, the words "empty string", non-empty strings or attributes, `{ }`, `()`. Causal: ablation barely changes the next token (KL 0.0017), so weak downstream effect at the prompt end. Note: one extra run_prompt attempt was blocked as too close to pool phrasing and never executed; 4 ran.
causal: Zero-ablating the feature on a Python snippet ending in `return ""` (active at 30-35 on all three empty-string tokens) left the next-token distribution almost unchanged: newline 0.964 -> 0.954, KL 0.0017, log-prob deltas at active positions <= 0.004.
examples_explanation: Fires on the empty-string literal token in code: every top example peaks on ` ""` (space + two double quotes) as an assigned, returned, default or JSON value. Promoted tokens are also empty-string forms (` ""`, `:""`, `("")`). I expect it to generalise, somewhat weaker, to single-quote `''` and to no-space variants like `=""`. Should NOT fire on non-empty strings or attribute values (style="..."), ordinary quotes in prose, other code punctuation, exceptions/null-ish code without an empty literal, math/LaTeX, citations, or plain prose and numbers.
surprises: All three sets predicted 0 for "}$$ $$\begin{aligned} P_{3,2}=\nu_4" but it fired at rel 0.153 with peak_token "$\" (a LaTeX miss no explanation covers), and label/examples also predicted 0 for "Fig. 1 curve [*c* ]{}shows a plot" which fired at rel 0.227 on peak_token "{}" (only investigated caught it, expected 2). Largest magnitude gap among hits: ".SourceManager, call, \"\")); assert(!err);" expected 8 in examples vs rel 0.577 on peak_token " \"\"));".

label: expressions of liking or affection
explanation: Fires on the verb "like" in its preference sense (like/likes/liked), peaking on the verb token itself. Tiers: "I like"/"likes"/"do you like" 0.8-1.0 of max; "liked", "don't like", "would like" 0.65-0.75; "dislike", German "mögen" (even in a bare word list), Spanish "gusta" 0.5; noun "likes", "likable", quoted mention of "like" 0.4; "mag" 0.4. Weak or off: filler "like" 0.15, "enjoys" 0.17, and zero on comparative "looks like", "Unlike", "love", "prefers". The token after the verb often carries a 0.1-0.4 spill. So it is lexical (the like-verb and its translations), not affection generally. Ablating it on "Personally, I like" shifted next-token mass from " to" toward " the"/" a", KL 0.09.
causal: Zero-ablating feature 4678 on "Everyone has different tastes. Personally, I like" (active only on " like", act 37.7) dropped " to" from 0.33 to 0.22 and " my" from 0.07 to 0.03 while " the" and " a" rose, KL 0.0945: a modest shift away from the "like to do / like my X" preference-verb continuations.
examples_explanation: Fires on the verb "like" in its preference sense (" like", " likes", " liked"), right on that token, after a subject: "I like X", "he likes music", "a person who likes to...". All eight top examples peak on like/likes at 38-40; promoted tokens are liked/likes/dislike/gusta. Expect strongest for first-person or third-person "like(s)" plus object or "to" infinitive, slightly weaker for past "liked". Uncertain, weak guesses: "like" quoted as a filler word, and German "mögen" in a modal-verb list. Should NOT fire on "love" or other positive sentiment without the verb like, comparative/preposition "like", nor on code, citations, or technical prose lacking the word.
surprises: Label set's only false positive was "the concepts of peace, love, and brotherhood" (expected 3 on "love", actual rel 0, peak_token "."), and it under-called "He likes to make food" (expected 6, actual rel 0.989, peak_token " likes") and "\"I like to share with you.\"" (expected 7, actual rel 1.025, peak_token " like"). Investigated set's only miss was the agent sentence "I love tea and my sister prefers strong black coffee." (expected 0, actual rel 0.1 right at the firing threshold, peak_token " prefers"), and it over-called "mögen. Nun kann man" (expected 5, actual rel 0.309, peak_token " mögen").

label: conditional statements and possibilities in reasoning or argumentation
explanation: Fires on restrictive "only" (also "sole") when it marks the single possible option or outcome, and on the words completing that construction (the following verb, noun, "is/was", "to", "if"). Tiers: ~0.7 of max on "could only mean"; 0.35-0.45 on "only possible if", "can only wonder", "has only a single purpose", "sole hope ... was to"; 0.12-0.25 on plain "the only road ... was", "had only three", trailing "taxes only". Does NOT fire: conditionals without "only" (if/unless/might), "just/merely", "the one spot ... is if", "may bring only two", sentence-initial "Only then"/"only four", code. Even "works only if" gave 0. Causal: ablation barely matters (KL 0.006).
causal: Zero-ablating the feature on "A triangle with those angles is possible only" (active at 22.6 on " only") lowered p(" if") only from 0.810 to 0.782 with KL 0.0062, so it nudges toward "if" but the model barely relies on it there.
examples_explanation: Fires on restrictive/exclusive "only" stating a necessary condition or sole possibility: "only possible if", "possible only if", "could only mean". Peak sits on " only" itself, or on the word right after it ("only [[possible]]"). The direction promotes " only", " either", " unless", so it is about exclusivity/limitation rather than conditionals in general. Strongest after modals or in reasoning ("can only", "the only way/place ... is if"); weaker expected for quantity "only one man" and trailing "by violence only". Not expected to fire on code, hex constants, product lists, medical or travel prose without "only", or on a bare "if" lacking an exclusivity word. Based on top examples only; nothing was run.
surprises: Investigated missed two firings: "only one man left, the lieutenant himself" (expected 1.5, actual rel 0.228, peak_token ",") and the agent-written "If the river floods again, we might move unless the council builds a levee." (expected 0, actual rel 0.12, peak_token "."), the latter contradicting the claim that conditionals without "only" do not fire. Label/examples sets got firing right but named "only" as the peak when it was actually " is" ("The only way ... is to", "the only place ... is if"), "," ("by violence only,") or " think" ("I can only think"), giving peak_hit 0.167.

label: programming-related keywords and structures
explanation: Fires on code tokens that open a NAMED parameter/placeholder slot, not on code in general. Strong (0.6-0.8 of max): regex named groups "(?P" (P 0.78-0.83, "=" 0.56), SQL "IN"/"OUT" parameter modes (0.68/0.47), ",'" before a second call argument (0.74), the word "parameter" inside a code string (0.61), "<arg name=\"" (0.41-0.58), SQL bind " :" (0.56). Mid (0.25-0.4): GraphQL "($", macro "NAME(" openers. Weak (0.1-0.2): "parameter"/"argument" in prose, non-param name= attributes, Elixir " :atom". Zero: plain function signatures, PHP "($", Haskell types, math, comments, prose. Causal: ablation at "(?P" barely moves the output (KL 0.0003), so it is a readout, not a driver there.
causal: Zero-ablating 12043 on a regex prompt ending in "(?P" (feature active at 26.0 on the final "P") left the next-token distribution essentially unchanged: p("<") 0.9896 -> 0.989, KL 0.0003, so the model does not rely on it for that prediction.
examples_explanation: The top examples do not support the broad "programming keywords" label. The feature peaks where a named parameter or argument is about to be given: the `,'` after `window.open(url` (window-name argument), ` ($` opening a GraphQL variable list (`subscription ($clientId`), and the word "parameter" in "Missing parameter %s". The promoted tokens (propOrder, HasForeignKey, invokingState) are identifier-like. I expect it to fire on parameter declarations and placeholders (SQL `IN col`, `:email`, `<param name=`, `($`), weakly on other code punctuation, and not on prose, citations, maths, legal text or code comments.
surprises: Investigated over-predicted "TopResults(IN col varchar(64), IN limited int(3)" (expected 6, actual rel 0.252, peak_token " IN") and "<param name=\"LSU_order\"" (expected 6.5, actual rel 0.39, peak_token " name" not "=\""), and falsely predicted firing on "<string name=\"action" (expected 2, actual 0). Label/examples sets both false-fired on "<?php echo json_encode($" (expected 5/3, actual 0) and examples missed "(?P=rpt))" (expected 1, actual rel 0.768, peak_token "P"); label named the wrong peak token on every firing row (peak_hit 0).

label: URLs and reference identifiers
explanation: Fires inside URL query strings, not on URLs in general. Strongest (0.8-0.96 of max) on tracking parameters in percent-encoded links: "utm", "_", "medium", "campaign", "=". Generic key=value&key=value parameters reach 0.3-0.4 (peak on "=" or the key). Weak tier, 0.12-0.2: JATS-style {ref-type="..."} attributes ("ref", "-", "type"), article-URL tails like /full#anchor-name, escaped ":\/\/" in JSON, CDN hostnames. Zero on scheme, host and path of ordinary URLs, snake_case identifiers outside URLs (user_id), LaTeX subscripts, and prose. Top examples also show it on mid-document <bos>, which I could not test. Causal: zero-ablating it at a "&utm" prompt left the next-token distribution unchanged (KL 0.0001), so no measurable output role there.
causal: Zero-ablating feature 2788 on a percent-encoded URL ending in "&utm" (active at 12 positions, up to 31.05) left the next-token prediction unchanged ("_" 0.9967 -> 0.9966, KL 0.0001), with per-position log-prob shifts between -0.56 and +0.55.
examples_explanation: Top examples are dominated by a mid-context <bos> token (document boundary), which cannot occur inside pool sentences. The only in-text example peaks on "_" inside a URL-encoded query string (utm_source), so I expect weaker firing inside URL query parameters, paths and fragments, and possibly on markup reference anchors like (#t0010){ref-type=...}. Similar features (URL / web-link / code syntax) support this. I expect NO firing on ordinary prose (news, legal, medical, restaurant text), plain list numbering, LaTeX fragments, or a bare "([Table" without the anchor identifier.
surprises: All three sets predicted firing on "\"></script> <link href=\"https://maxcdn.bootstrapcdn.com" (label expected 7, examples 3, investigated 2, on "cdn") but actual was 0 (peak_token "\"></"), the only false positive in every set. The label set also overshot the weak tier, e.g. "([Table 2](#t0010){ref-type=\"table" expected 6 vs rel 0.194 with peak_token "ref", while investigated undershot "type=artist&page=3\",\"next\":..." (expected 3.5 vs rel 0.542, peak_token "=") and missed peaks on ".00552/full#supplementary-material>" (peak_token "#", predicted "-") and the utm sentence (peak_token "source", predicted "_").

label: technical terms related to communication systems and leadership styles
explanation: Fires across the body of a definition or descriptive gloss: the words that say what a thing is or does after "X refers to the...", "is a device that...", "in which...", "whose ... depends on". It is sustained over the whole clause and resets to zero at the period. Label's leadership/communication topic is incidental. Tiers: 0.6-0.8 of max late in a "refers to" definition (peak on "towards"), 0.4-0.7 in "that/whose/in which" clauses and headless definition fragments, 0.15-0.35 on follow-up elaborations ("may include ... where"). Zero on the defined term and "is a", narrative, dates/sport, code, arithmetic questions, abstract-style method claims. Ablation barely changes predictions (KL 0.009). One extra run_prompt attempt was blocked by the permission classifier and never ran.
causal: Zero-ablating the feature on "Servant leadership refers to the ability of a manager to guide employees towards" (active on 9 positions, up to 17.5) left the next-token distribution almost unchanged (KL 0.009; " the" 0.19 -> 0.18, " achieving" 0.14 -> 0.13), so the feature tracks definition context without measurably driving the output here.
examples_explanation: All top examples are one repeated sentence: "...leadership refers to the leader's skills to influence others [[towards]] achieving goals", so the evidence is thin. My reading: the feature fires inside the body of a definitional/encyclopedic gloss (the text explaining what a term is, after "refers to"/"is a"), peaking on the function word or verb that continues the defining clause (towards, to, in which, that, whose, involving). The label's "communication systems and leadership" topic is probably incidental. Not expected to fire: code, math problems, citations, sports/date facts, quotes and news, conversational text, or abstract-style sentences that report results rather than define a concept.
surprises: Investigated's only firing error was a false positive on "conditions in a periurban area served by the Family Health Program" (expected 2 on "served", actual 0, peak_token "conditions"), and it over-predicted "keys that are in one set but not the other. In reconciliation, the difference is" (expected 5 on "other", actual rel 0.236 with peak_token " difference", i.e. after the period, contradicting the claimed reset). Peak location was mostly missed across all sets (e.g. "whose value depends on a voltage or current elsewhere in" peaked on " in", not "value"/"depends"; label set missed "an activity that obeys the rules" at rel 0.374, peak_token " rules", and "violent actions involving animated characters" at rel 0.282, peak_token " character").

label: numerical data and statistical references
explanation: Fires on the SECOND digit of a publication year inside an author-year citation (digits are single tokens: the "0" of 2014, the "9" of 1998), decaying over the third digit (~0.25) and fourth (~0.08). Tiers: "Author et al. 20xx" 0.7-0.85 of max; "et al., 19xx", "Author (2006)", "Author 2013" 0.55-0.65; pandoc keys like [@Name2003] and markdown-link years 0.3-0.45; bibliography "Surname, First M. 1987." 0.2-0.26; "et al. in 2016" 0.15. Does NOT fire on plain years in prose (1945, 1990s), "Table 2019", statistics, percentages, sample sizes, scores, numeric ranges or bracketed [12] references, so the label is wrong. Causal: ablation barely changes the next token (KL 0.005).
causal: Zero-ablating feature 115 on "... earlier work (Keller et al. 2014" (active at 55.3 on the year's "0", 16.9 on "1", 5.0 on "4") barely moved the next-token distribution: KL 0.0049, with ";" dropping 0.239 -> 0.205 and ")." rising 0.280 -> 0.299, so the feature marks the citation-year position but the model's closing-punctuation prediction hardly depends on it.
examples_explanation: Fires on the year inside an academic in-text citation, peaking on the year's second digit (the "0" of 20xx, the "9" of 19xx). All eight top examples are "Author et al. YEAR" in parenthetical citation lists, so the label "numerical data and statistics" is too broad. Expect strongest after "et al." plus a year; weaker for years in other citation formats (citation keys like @Dujmic2008, markdown bib links, reference-list entries such as "Timothy C. 2011."). Expect no firing on non-citation numbers (sports scores, cell counts, list numbers, footnote digits), code, or ordinary prose without years.
surprises: Investigated's largest miss was the agent sentence "Okonkwo (2004) argued that the sample mean was 20.5 with n = 1998." (expected 6, actual rel 0.135, peak_token "0"), and examples overshot "*, 2002](#bib8){ref-type=\"other\"})." (expected 7, actual rel 0.113, peak_token "0"). The label set false-fired on four random numeric rows, worst "4–6, 7–5, 6–0 against Nicole Arendt" (expected 4, actual 0, peak_token "4"), and got peak_hit 0 because it named whole years like "2003" while the peak is the single digit "0".

label: terms related to counterfactual reasoning and concepts in quantum mechanics
explanation: Not counterfactuals or quantum mechanics. Fires diffusely across expository prose about abstract mathematical objects and definitions (probability, analysis, linear algebra), peaking on concept nouns: "sample space" 0.67 of max, "distribution" 0.71, "measurable" 0.73, "greatest lower bound" 0.64, "eigenspace" 0.63; surrounding function words sit at 0.3-0.5. Weak tier (0.15-0.3) on symbol-heavy LaTeX and counting statements. Zero on everyday "space" (office, parking, outer), everyday counterfactuals, programming advice, quantum-computing news prose, biology, and section headings; "Let $f$ be..." openers barely fire (under 0.2). Causal: zeroing it on a sample-space definition prompt changed nothing measurable (KL 0.0003, " space" stayed at 0.992), so no evidence it drives the next-token prediction there.
causal: Zero-ablating feature 312 on "In probability theory, a random variable is a measurable function defined on the sample" (active at 12 of 15 positions, up to 15.5) left the next-token prediction unchanged (" space" 0.9919 -> 0.9922, KL 0.0003), with the largest per-position effect a -0.36 log-prob shift at " on", so the probe shows no causal role in this prediction.
examples_explanation: Evidence is thin: all 8 top examples are the same text, peaking on " space" in "function from a sample space". The label (counterfactuals, quantum mechanics) is not supported by anything shown. Best guess: fires on "space" as a mathematical object noun (sample space, probably null space / vector space), strongest right after "sample". Similar features point to maths/logic text, so weak sub-threshold activity on other abstract maths nouns (function, bound, set) is possible. Density 0.56% suggests it is somewhat broader than this one phrase, but I cannot tell how. Expected NOT to fire: code, imports, prose narrative, news, biology, section headers, and LaTeX formulas with no named space.
surprises: Investigated's largest miss was "which is a polygon consisting of $2\# (V\cap R^a_+" (expected 2 on "consisting", actual rel 0.644 with peak_token " of"), and "cover, it is rather the largest lower bound of all these numbers" was over-predicted (expected 4.5 on "bound", actual rel 0.18, peak_token " numbers"). The label set missed the same polygon row (expected 0) plus "surjective function between a sample space $S$" (expected 1, actual rel 0.649, peak_token " space"), and falsely predicted firing on "cybersecurity-breaking schemes, even on these early machines" (expected 2, actual 0).

label: situations involving crisis or urgency in a narrative context
explanation: Fires across the "reveal" clause of a narrative: the words stating what someone unexpectedly discovers, notices or finds, starting at the discovery cue (realized, learns that, found, "to my dismay/surprise", "inside was", "there stood") and persisting through the revealed content. Tiers seen in my own prompts: 0.55-0.7 of max on a staged reveal ("there stood my", "inside was nothing", "were gone", "dismay"); 0.3-0.45 on plot-synopsis discoveries and all-caps "LOOKED INSIDE"; 0.15-0.3 trailing tokens. Zero on crisis/urgency without a reveal (emergency, evacuation, "Hurry"), on news claims, and on non-narrative "instead/actually/exactly", so the label is wrong. Causally weak: ablation barely changed the next-token distribution (KL 0.004).
causal: Zeroing feature 11411 on "I unzipped my backpack to grab my lunch, and to my surprise the sandwich was" (active at 0.2-0.47 of max from "my surprise" onward) left the next-token distribution almost unchanged, " gone" 0.286 -> 0.268 and " missing" 0.125 -> 0.118, KL 0.0038.
examples_explanation: The label looks wrong: this is narrative surprise/reveal, not crisis. Top examples peak on the verb that delivers an unexpected discovery after a setup ("to see if it was wet and out [[comes]] the tiniest"; "noticed I was holding an empty leash. My dog [[had]] slipped"). Promoted tokens (instead, actually, exactly, なんと) fit a "turns out, surprisingly" reading. Expect firing on discovery/twist constructions: "only to discover he was", "UNTIL I OPENED IT! Much to my chagrin ... is filled", "discovers the prisoner is", "In its place was a note instead". Should not fire on code, math, category lists, headlines, plain exposition, or opinion/chat without a reveal. Peak-token guesses are uncertain (reveal verb vs discovery verb).
surprises: Firing was predicted correctly but magnitudes were overestimated and peak tokens mostly missed: the label set expected 7 on "discovers" for "Until one day he discovers the prisoner is a beautiful princess" but actual rel was 0.267 with peak_token " a", and its only false positive was "claimed responsibility for the death" (expected 2, actual 0). Peaks landed late or on punctuation rather than the discovery cue, e.g. ", UNTIL I OPENED IT! Much to my chagrin" peaked on "," (rel 0.31), "In its place was a note instead saying" on "”." (rel 0.299), and "Gone were my keys, I realized" on "." (rel 0.26, expected on "realized").

label: words and phrases that consistently appear multiple times in relation to quantities or time duration
explanation: Lexical feature for the token " over"/" Over" (with leading space), in every sense. Tiers: preposition of duration/space/preference and legal "over his objection" ~1.0 of max; math "space over a field" 0.83; sentence-initial "Over" 0.75-0.88; particle "gave ... over to" 0.76; quantity "over 40" and predicative "is over" ~0.61. Weak spillover onto the following token (0.08-0.45). Compounds barely fire: " Overview", " takeover", " overcame" ~0.10-0.12; "Overview" without leading space, " Overall", "moreover", "above", "across", "during", "throughout", "more than" = 0. Causal: ablation drops " over" after "over and" from 0.99 to 0.36. Note: one extra run_prompt attempt was blocked before running (it contained HTML resembling pool item 5); it returned no data.
causal: Ablating feature 2616 on "He practiced the same song over and" cut the next-token probability of " over" from 0.994 to 0.361 and made " again" the top prediction (0.004 to 0.575), KL 0.98.
examples_explanation: Token-level feature for the word " over". All eight top examples peak on " over" at near-identical strength (53-54) across senses: temporal ("over a few days"), spatial ("over large compost piles"), comparative ("one technique over another"), legal ("over his objection"), locative ("over in the School"). The label's quantity/duration framing is too narrow. Expect strong firing on any standalone " over" as preposition, slightly weaker for capitalised sentence-initial " Over", the particle use ("handed over") and the "more than" sense. Expect no firing on sentences without the word; "Overview" as a single token probably stays below threshold. Other prepositions, quantities and durations without "over" should not fire.
surprises: The only firing miss in all three sets was ".html\">Overview

label: past tense verbs indicating personal experiences or usage
explanation: Fires on first-person owner/user testimony, forum style: "I used to have one", "I have a...", "I've been using/had them", "Mine/Ours are...". Not a past-tense detector: it peaks on the possession/usage verb, its object, or a possessive pronoun, and smears across the rest of the clause. Tiers: 0.75-0.87 of max ("Ours", "using" after I've been, "have one"); 0.4-0.6 ("I've had", "I have a", "Been running it" with dropped subject); 0.2-0.35 (French "j'ai acheté", "I owned" in cold context, obligation "I have to"). Strongly context-boosted by preceding first-person ownership sentences. Silent on third-person narrative, news, finance, code, maths, and mostly on third-person possession. Causal: ablation did essentially nothing (KL 0.0001).
causal: Zero-ablating feature 4446 on "Does anyone still make these? I used to have one but sold it. Now I" (active on used..it, peak 12.5 on " have") left the next-token distribution unchanged (top tokens "'" 0.253, " want" 0.170 to 0.171), KL 0.0001, with per-position log-prob deltas all under 0.05.
examples_explanation: Fires on first-person statements of owning or having used a product/item, forum-review style: "I used to [[have]] one", "I have [[a]] stainless steel...". Peak lands on the possession verb or the token right after it (the article/object), once "I have/had/used (to have)" is established. Only two distinct top examples, so the breadth is inferred: I expect weaker firing for "I've used them", "Been using it", and third-person possession ("my wife has that"), and possibly French "j'ai". Should NOT fire on code, math, HTML, news prose, third-person narrative, finance text, or "have" as a pure auxiliary without an ownership/usage sense.
surprises: The label set missed "wetbag. Mine match because I am" (expected 1, actual rel 0.596, peak_token " Mine") and over-predicted "10) Been using it for a while and it works" (expected 8, actual rel 0.158, peak_token " for", also over-predicted at 5 by examples and investigated). All sets over-predicted "Genius I had a series 1" (label 6 / examples 8 / investigated 4 vs rel 0.178, peak_token " a"), and the investigated agent sentence "Ours broke after two winters" fired at rel 0.419 but peaked on " broke" rather than "Ours".
